text:
A classifier answers in one pass through its model. A language model writes its answer one token at a time, and every token is another pass. That's why generation is slow, and why it's hungry for memory. Four questions, all on one model: seventy billion parameters, served from eight GPUs.

Question one. Why is LLM inference split into prefill and decode? Because generating a response has two phases, with different bottlenecks. Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass. That's large matrix multiplication, so it's compute-bound, and it sets the time to first token, or TTFT. Decode then produces one token per step. Each step reads every weight and the whole cached context to do a little arithmetic, so it's bound by memory bandwidth, and it sets the time per output token. Count it. With a two-thousand-token prompt, prefill puts every weight it reads to work two thousand times. A decode step for one request uses it once. So the levers differ. A chat product cares most about TTFT and smooth streaming; an offline summarization job, about throughput and cost per request. Long prompts make prefill expensive, and long answers make decode expensive. The follow-up: users wait seconds before any text appears, and then it streams quickly. That's prefill. Shorten the prompt, or cache a long shared prefix. Waiting to fill a bigger batch first would only add delay. Every decode step also reads the cached context, and that cache is the part that grows.
